items.title: Aik Alif
items.description: An experimental documentary tracing a filmmaker’s return to Islam through Sufism. Through spiritual encounters, Bulleh Shah’s poetry, and abstract black-and-white visuals, the film discovers Islam’s theological multiplicities.
items.story: A personal exploration of faith and identity, this experimental documentary follows a filmmaker's spiritual journey as he reconnects with Islam as an adult through the mystical tradition of Sufism. The filmmaker finds himself questioning his relationship with Allah and understanding that Islam is not a monolithic religion. Through intimate interactions with two Sufi practitioners, the film reveals an alternative understanding of Islam—one that emphasizes inner exploration, devotion, poetic wisdom, and direct spiritual experience over rigid adherence to Islamic law. The central narrative is anchored by the poetry of Bulleh Shah, the 19th-century Sufi poet whose verses form the heart of the film's musical composition 'Aik Alif,' teaching that 'all is one.' Shot in black and white, the film weaves together personal reflection, mystical philosophy, and Kira Winter’s art.

items.title: Do You Remember?
items.description: Blending narrative, memory, and family archives, a filmmaker confronts childhood abuse, using storytelling as a path to healing and reclaiming his lost memories of childhood.
items.story: This experimental documentary follows a filmmaker as he confronts the lack of memories surrounding his childhood abuse. Through a deeply personal process of storytelling, he uses narrative as a means of regaining memory and piecing together a fractured past. Blending family archives, interviews, and artistic collaborations, the film moves fluidly between memory and recreation, holding a space where pain and healing coexist.

items.story: The great East Window at St Anne’s, depicting the Crucifixion on a monumental scale, is over 150 years old and in urgent need of repair, and you can still support its conservation by sponsoring a pane through our ongoing appeal.

items.title: NOA
items.description: An experimental film exploring identity and motion...
items.story: The genesis of this film lies in a serendipitous meeting at a mental well-being workshop for Black men in East London, where, amidst painting paper hats and shared stories, I met Noa, a dancer whose movements spoke volumes about resilience and expression, leading to a collaboration exploring play—a concept often stripped from Black male experiences—through repeated dance performances in UCL's Black Box studio, using the camera as a tool of discovery to capture nuances of expression and silent dialogue, inspired by Maya Deren's cinematic philosophies to let dance narrate its own story, while navigating institutional resistance and creating a sanctuary within the studio, balancing authentic representation of Noa's artistry with my creative instincts, evolving from an initially silent, black-and-white piece to one enriched with the music that fuels his performances, acknowledging the inseparability of sound and movement in his expression.

collaboration.focus: Play and its absence in Black male experiences

items.title: Aberfeldy Estate
items.description: An exploration of regeneration through point clouds scattering.
items.story: The Aberfeldy Estate in Poplar, East London, is undergoing a significant transformation aimed at revitalising the area and addressing the city's housing challenges. In partnership with EcoWorld London, Poplar HARCA is redeveloping the estate into Aberfeldy Village, a mixed-use urban village that will include over 1,500 new homes, with approximately 39% designated as affordable housing. This redevelopment is particularly noteworthy in the context of London's social housing landscape. The project has faced scrutiny over concerns of gentrification and the displacement of existing residents. In early 2023, Tower Hamlets Council rejected the proposed plans, citing issues such as increased traffic and the potential for social cleansing. However, following a strong mandate from the estate's residents—93% of whom voted in favour of the redevelopment—the Mayor of London intervened, approving the next phase of the project. The Aberfeldy regeneration highlights the delicate balance between urban renewal and the preservation of affordable housing. While the development promises enhanced amenities and infrastructure, it underscores the broader debate in London about how to meet housing demands without eroding the social fabric of established communities. </br></br>As part of my project on the Aberfeldy Estate, I used 3D scanning to create a detailed point cloud of the site, capturing the geometry and spatial character of the buildings and surrounding public spaces. I then layered this visualisation with audio from the Tower Hamlets council meeting, where residents and officials debated the redevelopment plans. The result is an immersive audiovisual experience that juxtaposes the physical space of the estate with the social and political context of its transformation, highlighting the tensions around gentrification, affordable housing, and community engagement in London’s urban regeneration projects.

items.title: Archives Also Die
items.description: Caught in a maze of bureaucratic absurdity and colonial remnants, a British-Nigerian filmmaker reassembles their fractured identity through archival images, brutalist architecture, and experimental cinema—interrogating the power and politics of memory.
items.story: Growing up as “Peter” in the UK, I came of age at the intersection of administrative fiction and diasporic truth. The moment I received a citizenship letter in someone else’s name, I began an odyssey through bureaucracy—a journey that blurred the line between identity and absurdity. The archive became a mirror and a maze. This film is not only a retelling of that journey, but a confrontation with the very structures that mediate belonging, memory, and meaning. Archives Also Die is my attempt to reclaim voice through form—to juxtapose the rationalist facade of empire with the chaotic, affective, lived realities of postcolonial subjects. I did not want to merely critique the archive from afar, but to live within it—to screen record it, mispronounce its metadata, pixelate its hierarchies, and project it onto the walls of the present. My body and voice carry the friction between my ancestral name—Oluwatosin Oluwakayode Ominiyi Temi Tope Peter Adegoke—and the imposed simplicity of “Peter.” This film insists that representation is not enough. Transformation is necessary. Through tunnels, towers, and terminals, I offer a new passage through history—not to retrieve what was lost, but to reshape what remains.

items.title: Natural Architecture
items.description: Set within the storied landscape of Spain, this cinematic journey follows a community of apprentices, architects, and master engineers as they gather to reimagine architecture through stone...
items.story: Stone has stood at the heart of architecture since the dawn of civilisation. Over the past year, I have been collaborating with Rosal Stones, a stone extraction and fabrication company based in Caravaca, Spain. As part of a three-person team, we travelled across the rocky, sedimentary landscapes of Murcia, a region shaped largely by sandstone. The city’s natural beauty was striking. In observing its architecture, we noticed how vibrant hues such as sky blue and tangerine orange were applied to façades, infusing the built environment with warmth and a sense of well-being.

items.title: Black Mary’s Pleasure Garden
items.description: A poetic short film documenting the community-led unveiling of a memorial to 17th-century healer Mary Woolaston, where music, ritual, and dance become acts of remembrance and collective healing.
items.story: A short documentary film for the Black Mary Project (2025, King’s Cross), capturing the unveiling of a memorial sculpture for Mary Woolaston - a 17th-century Black healer whose well once served London’s poor. The film documents communal ritual, global majority musical performances, healing ceremonies, and collective dance, exploring how spiritual practice and embodied celebration can reclaim erased Black working-class histories.

items.title: the stone they lay
items.description: Hidden in plain sight, a set of stone benches in London becomes the vessel for a poetic excavation...
items.story: This project began as a modest exploration of historical street furniture: a set of stone benches dotted across the St Paul’s area, their presence anonymous and unremarked. Yet, these stones were extracted from the Thames Embankment wall, a site underpinned—literally—by Victorian engineering, sanitation systems, and layers of forgotten city planning. I found myself drawn to them, not just for what they were, but for what they contained—earth and water, stillness and memory. As I began filming, I worked through a double-diamond process—an approach borrowed from the tech world, where I once worked—which allowed me to ideate expansively before defining, and later to develop freely before distilling. This journey was not linear, but iterative and often uncertain. The core question was always this: how can the inanimate speak? Through image, sound design, and poetic structure, the film seeks to animate what cannot move, and to hold space for what no longer speaks. We follow the benches as portals between past and present, accompanied by soundscapes built from church bells, hydrophones submerged in the Thames, and EQ’d traffic noise woven into the whip pans between locations.

items.title: The Building Crafts College
items.description: We collaborated with the UK’s leading provider of Construction Crafts Education to create a film that told their story in an engaging and visually striking way. Our goal was to showcase not only the institution’s reputation and opportunities but also to capture the energy and ambition of the students they aim to inspire. To achieve this, we used drone cinematography to frame the urban landscape of Stratford, contrasting the area’s architectural evolution with the traditional skills being taught inside the classroom. The combination of sweeping aerial shots and close, human-focused storytelling gave the film both scale and intimacy, helping potential students see themselves as part of a bigger picture while still connecting on a personal level. The finished piece was more than just a promotional video; it was a cinematic narrative designed to elevate the brand, celebrate craftsmanship, and engage the next generation of construction professionals.

items.title: Material interrogation
items.description: Material Research
items.story: material interrogation, I created ice cubes using encapsulated silicone with handcrafted jewellery suspended inside. Ice, usually a fleeting and transient mineral, was subverted through the use of stable silicone, hoodwinking the observer and provoking questions of material perception. Silicone’s qualities, unmelting yet oddly bouncy, introduced further perceptual oddities. Jewellery, durable and permanent, appeared fragile, suspended in time. By translating an impermanent mineral into permanence, the piece highlights how extractive processes fuel gluttony; not only in consumption (jewellery as a symbol of that), but in our urge to preserve and manipulate minerals, resisting their impermanence.

items.title: Jewellery as Prop
items.description: Material Research
items.story: Made as jewellery props, the concrete pillows interrogate the presumptive relationship between form and material. A pillow conventionally evokes comfort and familiarity, yet here its weight and hardness provoke unease. This dissonance reflects how extractive materials permeate domestic life in ways we often overlook. Concrete, one of the most mineral-heavy substances, produces vast CO₂ emissions, making its translation into a soft, intimate object both absurd and confronting. By re-coding form through material contradiction, the work draws attention to how objects can be estranged, compelling us to reconsider their making, meaning, and ecological burden.

items.title: Hiraeth
items.description: Co-wrote, co-directed, and performed in Hiraeth, an ensemble-devised theatre piece exploring cultural identity and displacement through movement, rhythm, and abstraction rather than linear narrative.
items.story: Co-wrote, co-directed, and performed in Hiraeth, an avant-garde ensemble-devised theatre piece exploring cultural identity and belonging. Working collaboratively with the cast, we collected personal stories and created original poetry to investigate the question 'Who am I?' The production used movement, dance, and stark visual imagery to express displacement and cultural longing—eschewing linear narrative for a rhythm-based, gestural language. The devising process prioritized embodied storytelling over text, allowing personal histories to emerge through collective choreography and improvisation.

items.title: Climate Ambassadors
items.description: Climate Ambassadors is a Department for Education–funded initiative led by the University of Reading and EAUC that supports nurseries, schools, and colleges in creating Climate Action Plans to prepare young people for a green economy and help education settings respond to climate change.
items.story: [Project Ongoing] Climate Ambassadors is an initiative funded by the Department for Education with the aim of helping all education settings make and implement a Climate Action Plan. The initiative is led by the University of Reading and EAUC and is delivered by a consortium of organisations across England. By supporting nurseries, schools and colleges to build their climate action plans, Climate Ambassadors can help to ensure that young people have access to the learning and skills they will need for their future in the green economy while also helping education settings meet the challenges of a changing climate.
